words: I feel like I'm a card dealer dealing out interviewers.

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: Yeah, that's the way card dealers do.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: I was just with Agnes for two hours and she's a wonderful person.

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: She is a wonderful person.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: She kept saying, "I want you to go meet Myrtle, she's a wonderful person."

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: Yeah, I met [her] over at the hospital. Her and I worked over there together, that's where I met Agnes. My husband, Todd, over here, he met her daughter. He liked her daughter real well, the one that's out in the orchard.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: Can I ask about the paintings?

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: Yeah. That's painted in 1815, hand painted. They didn't have cameras in those days, you see, and you sat for your por traits, you know. Just like we do; we go downtown and sit for our pictures. 3

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: Oh, they had beautiful frames on it at one time, but the horses give out so they took the frames off and threw them away.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: Can you imagine what the frames would be like?

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: They were beautiful frames, but I have never seen them. Wherever they went, wherever we lived as a family, they hung that up, the picture, they hung it up. My cousin and I was talking about it and I said, "Well, you know what it means to me, Ethel?" She said, "No." And I said, "Well, it means home to me," I said, "you know, wherever my grandparents lived, why, they always had those pictures hanging up." And that meant home to us. And she has one over in Portland. She has a painting and her's is a lady, a woman with a bonnet on. This is Sam Cordis and the other is ...

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: That's just beautiful!

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: Well, yeah. They should be kept, and my children that live in San Francisco, they want it, they said they'll take care of it. So, I'm glad to know that they want it and will take care of it.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: They'll take it.

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: Yeah, that's right. You know, we're not here on earth very long and then somebody else will have to care for it.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: You want to know, don't you? 4

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: I don't care who has it just as long as somebody will take care of it. It's just the idea that somebody will take care of it.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: My father's got a book that I love by Charles Dickens; it's A Christmas Carol. He read it to us every Christmas when we were young and I said I wanted that book and it's so old now. It's so worn, so he told me when he died I get the book and I was so excited that he would give that to me.

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: Here's a book that I'm interested in too. Now, my mother was a very young girl way up this Clearwater River. Why, there was a miner there that just mined and he was out there and good land sakes away from civilization all together, and what do you supposed he did? He got that and gave it to my mother when she was about 15. And you know I think an awful lot of that. Now, there he was way out there in the woods. It didn't make any difference where he was, he still had a little culture.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: He sure did.

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: He loved the finer things. If you notice in there in some of those, he underlined them.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: It doesn't say when the book was published, does it? 5

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: No, I don't know anything about the book. I asked my mother if I couldn't have it on account of it was so old and he had given it to her. I imagine, you know, he liked her and so he give her that book.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: It looks like he's underlined things that really meant a lot to him.

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: Yeah, that's right. He underlined clear things. Sometimes I read the things that he underlined.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: This is interesting. Does it tell you a little more about him?

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: Well, yeah. It tells even as simple a life as he led, he still had a little culture, you know, the finer things in life. Even if they were miners and lived a rough life.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: Things were important to them.

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: Yeah. It's old; I don't know if it's worth anything, but that doesn't make any difference. And I must write this, you see, he writes this on here: "To make habitually a new estimate, that is an elevation." All those little things he marked, but there was one here that especially that I liked. One here I liked real well was in love. 6

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: There was one I remember hearing.

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: All the world loves a lover?

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: Yeah, that's it.

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: You wouldn't think that even a miner would have things like that.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: Isn't it a pretty cover, too?

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: Unusual. This looks like a piece of leather here and this funny board, and there's not a thing written in it, not a thing. No date or anything. Why don't people put dates on things?

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: I don't know.

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: I've got to write something in that because you know that's too bad. Now my children won't have any idea; they wouldn't have any idea where that come from without I told them.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: Right.

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: There isn't a thing in there. And if it wasn't for me, my mother telling me where it come from, I wouldn't know where it come from either. 7

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: What was your husband's name?

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: Harry Warren.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: How did you meet?

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: Oh, he come to my house every noon. He was a schoolteacher.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: He was a schoolteacher?

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: Yes, he taught for 22 years, did nothing else, didn't want to do anything else. He just liked teaching school.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: Did your parents like him?

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: No.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: They didn't?

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: No. They had another man that was better fixed than he was because he just taught school. But I didn't think anything about it. You can never tell; children don't always do like parents want them to.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: That's right; that's still happening. 8

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: I think, though, the reason Dad did it was that he was a finer one, that was all. He liked the finer things of life and I suppose most of us do, I don't know. Sometimes, now, I feel like just throwing all this stuff out and just living in a, you know, just simple because I've lived that way and I liked it. But, of course, I'll just live here like I have. You wonder sometimes and I think parents do that because they want their children to have ...

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: They want the best.

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: Yeah, that's right, they want the best for their children and that's the reason why they do that, because their finances look a little better than this man. Well, this man, they wanted me to marry, well, he was quite well to do at that time, consider ing. Of course, Harry was just starting out teaching school. He thought the other one was better, he didn't say too much about it, but he let you know.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: Did you and your husband talk about how many children you wanted to have?

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: No, we thought we'd have two or three, three or four; but, we only had that one. I had kind of a tragic ... I don't know, I lost one afterwards. I didn't have a doctor and I thought maybe there was something wrong. I never had any more children. Now, 9 whether that miscarriage caused that or I wasn't supposed to have them, of course, I never knew. When we were living out on that mountain at [unintelligible] and it was about 30 miles from town and it was about zero weather and we had about three feet of snow and the doctor wasn't going to take any trips. He'd had to come horseback. We had roads in those days, but they was underneath the snow and they didn't plow them out like they do and they didn't have cars. Cars got stuck in the snow, so they just didn't get over there. So, he didn't come out. I let him know, I wrote to him or had somebody phone for him, I don't remember. I think I wrote to him that I was ailing and he just wrote back and said he thought I had lost a child and he never said anything about corning out.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: Did most people have their children at home, then?

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: Yes, they did in those days. They don't allow them to do it anymore and it's not. good.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: Was your husband able to be right there with you when you had your baby?

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: Yeah, he was there. Of course, he was gone in the daytime, but he was there at night. Now, we had plans; we had the older child, you see, and we had plans on Harry going up to Moscow and going to school the next winter. We did make it, we went up to Moscow and went to school the next winter and I was supposed to 10 have the baby up there, you see, and have it in the hospital. But, I lost the baby before I was up in Moscow. We planned, you see, we planned lots of things.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: Yeah, you plan things and then things happen.

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: What is it, the best laid plans of mice and men all go astray?

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: Can you think of any particular reasons why you got married? Did you have reasons why you wanted to get married?

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: No, we didn't have any. We were just in love, I guess. We went down here in Lewiston, we were married there. We lived up the, uh ... I've been outdoors working. We lived way up on Bear Ridge at that time, that's where he was teaching, on Bear Ridge. He taught school and went to school, taught school and went to school. And when this baby was to be born, we were going up to Moscow. We were saving up money, you see, saving up money to go to Moscow so he could get more education. I don't think he was getting a degree at that time -- he did finally get a degree, but not at that time. We lived up in Moscow the next winter. I wasn't very well all the rest of the winter. That next winter, I wasn't very well, but we lived up there and he went to school. He worked awful hard. He got good grades but he worked hard. 11

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: Yeah, I'm trying to help my husband through school now.

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: Yeah. Now, I could've worked if I hadn't of had this small child. I could have worked. But in those days, you didn't hire and in those days they didn't have places [where] they were kept like they do now. And I could've done it that way but I didn't. We just went up there on top of that mountain and we only paid $5 a month rent, so we could save money. But, of course, we spent it all, too. The next winter we spent it all. Then, we went to ... and then it was getting hard times and the schools themselves consolidated and then, he went up to Moscow, and then he went up to Kamiah, east Kamiah, and he taught there, but they were going to consolidate. They were getting better roads, you see, so you could go into Kamiah.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: How did he feel about consolidation?

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: Well, he just took it as a matter of fact, and I think he thought it was all right. I don't remember him ever saying anything.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: I did the [unintelligible] at the presentation.

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: Yeah, I remember that. It sure made me think of our days.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: I just love reading about those days. 12

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: Yeah, I do, too. I enjoyed those days. We lived simple but just the same. You don't have Literary Society. Have you ever read anything about Literary Society?

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: No, I haven't.

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: It's just simply, they call it Literary Society, but I don't think there is any society to it. They went every so often and had programs in school. Now, you see, they didn't have tele vision and radio -- nothing. We had nothing except for what little music that people did themselves. That's all we had. So, you see, we turned to little things and we had programs. Now, when we were on [unintelligible] Creek, we had Literary Society every so often. I don't know whether it was once a week or whether it was once a month. I can't remember. But they had programs, they had little dialogues they called them dialogues in those days, and now I think they call them something else.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: We call them dialogues, too, the thing we did in the presen tation between the two sisters right at the end -- we called that the dialogue. Now, you are right, I don't think too many people say dialogue.

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: What do they call them? They call them something else.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: Readings? 13

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: No, they aren't readings. Readings are when you do it by yourself. Yeah, we had readings and they had little ... where you had news. You'd get up and tell the news that happened all around. You had to be awful careful; they had to be edited be cause sometimes people put mean things in there. You had to be careful what you read. Well, we always had them, but you ought to stay away from them as much as you can. I remember on [unin telligible] Creek, they had people that wouldn't speak to one another, yet they'd be in a dialogue together. There is some thing else they called the dialogue, these little short plays. Yeah, something like you did down there, only the grown-ups would do it and they called it Literary Society. Then come Christmas time -- they'd have millions of big programs. Oh, they would have a great big program and every child had to take a part in it. It didn't make any difference whether he knew anything; he had to do it.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: Did everybody enjoy it?

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: Oh yes, because that's all they had. Now at Red Fir, they had lots of programs and they had people there, they was from other countries and they'd see them there all the time and there was pretty, beautiful music. We all enjoyed that because music was something, you know, that we didn't have. You didn't have it in your home unless you made it yourself. 14

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: Did you have brothers and sisters?

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: Yeah, I have a brother.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: When you are thinking back to your childhood, can you remem ber, like did your parents treat you differently from your brother?

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: I hardly remember anything.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: Did you do the same chores?

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: Well, he did outside chores and I did inside chores, but we learned how to do one another's chores, so if something happened and he didn't get home, I would do his chores. Like taking care of the cows, we all pitched in and did it. And if somebody went away or was away doing something or didn't get home in time, well, we could all do the chores. I can't ever remember feeling that I was ever put out. I can't remember that at all. And under privileged -- I never thought I was underprivileged. Now you hear that word an awful lot. And this low income -- it was never thought -- we never said that either.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: Sounds like you were pretty self-sufficient.

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: We were, and after we went on payroll wage in 1910 we had neighbors, they lived just exactly the way we did. The money, 15 they might have managed it differently, but we never had that high or low income, or underprivileged. I never heard that word until we grew up.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: Do you think your parents have influenced you in any way in your way of thinking?

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: Oh yes, I think they did. They taught me how to work and I think that's important. Now it was simple things because I have very little education, but they taught us how to do simple things. Like spading, we knew how to spade, we knew how to hoe, we knew how to pull weeds, we pulled, we knew one weed from another. We could go out in the woods and tell you all the different plants and everything. I remember going up to Glacier Park and people were asking me because they knew that I come from out in the woods and they asked me the different names of plants and things and I was right because my mother taught them to me. And her parents were mining people, but they studied the plants and they liked them.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: I just love plants.

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: I do, too, and I used to raise hundreds of them but I don't raise them anymore.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: They take a lot of time. 16

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: Yeah, they do, and I thought I had to have a certain kind of gravel and put gravel in the bottom of the little pot, see. I did a lot of little things that was unnecessary, I guess. But I wanted to do it right and I enjoyed handling the dirt. My husband fished and wherever we could go, he went fishing and I gathered stuff for my plants. I gathered certain kinds of coarse gravel and I gathered this dust for, sawdust, to do in and, you know, you learn lots of things about dirt. Sometimes, I got ticks on me, too. I don't like ticks.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: I don't either. Do you think there was any one thing or something special that you've done to support your family? I don't mean necessarily financial support, but anything to help out.

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: I turned everything I could make into a dollar. We raised chidkens and lived off the land. Now, I remember we lived at [unintelligible] during the depression and that was back in '35 or in '29, the markets all went broke. From that time on it was kind of hard for several years there. We raised everything we ate. Well, I liked it and it helped our finances. And I remember our . grocery bill when we lived in [unintelligible]. We had an acre of ground and we were paid about nine months out of the year, and I know that we always raised a garden. I can remember in the summertime when the garden was on and the chickens was laying e~gs, lots of times our bill for the month was under $5.00. But 17 we were careful and we lived off that. We had an acre of ground and we had three or four apple trees and then we had strawberries and we had raspberries and the chickens and we lived off of that. That's what we lived off of. We did that because it helped our finances.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: Did you ever enter any of your quilts in the fair?

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: No.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: You never did?

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: Never thought I had any that were good enough.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: You would've probably taken first prize.

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: Well, I took some lessons down at the "Ytl about quilting and I enjoyed every minute of that. There was a woman who had. given lessons on quilting and she had beautiful quilts, too.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: I would love to learn how to quilt.

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: It's just practice, practice, and practice.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: You have to have patience.

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: Yeah, that's right, a lot of patience. 18

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: It's all handwork, isn't it?

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: Well, I'd rather it would be. I make mine all handwork. That's a real quilt. If you're going to quilt a quilt, it's easier to quilt it when it's hand quilted. If you sew on the sewing machine you have to sew through that and that's too hard. It's so hard that you can't get in there to it.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: Do you do other things besides quilt? You crochet, too, don't you?

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: But I do crochet, too. I've got a sweater in here somewhere. Oh, that's crochet, I was looking at one thing and you were look ing at another. That's knit and I've got another one over there started. I knit one for my daughter-in-law. I've got a white sweater in there I did.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: Did you embroider these?

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: Oh yes, and see, that's padding all around and I've got stacks of those.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: Do you put this one on?

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: I put it on the sewing machine. No, that one is crocheted on. 19

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: You have so much talent!

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: That's crocheted on, but I have some where I quilted them on.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: We'll have to get you some to enter in a fair. Did you make this quilt? Did you make that pillow?

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: Oh, yes. I ought to make some more, I guess; and I knit that afghan over there.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: I love the colors, it looks so warm.

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: Well now, there are pieces that are left over, those pieces. One time, I made my jacket out of that green and I made a jacket and of course I had pieces left over, and you don't waste pieces.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: Isn't that neat? I love the quilt you have that uses the different pieces of dresses.

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: They are all my clothes, all of them are. Sometimes, yes, they meant a lot to us.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: That's your family right there on a quilt?

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: That'r right, and I have a quilt in here that I put all my 20 places that I lived. That's the top -- I lived there one winter and that's the [unintelligible] Creek. And this is about up the river, about 35 miles. Yeah, and I embroidered this. That's where Harry and I first met and that's where we got married. And then we come down here and lived and went to school down here. That's Kamiah. Now, this is when my son was in Alaska. That's Stites, we lived four years in Stites. We lived on [unintelli gible] Creek one winter. Now this is where my son lived in [unintelligible]. My daughter-in-law wants this. [Several more sentences which are mostly unintelligible.] This woman was mar- ried about 40 years, so I had to make a bigger quilt. But, that's a good thing for people to make; if you're young, a family, and they are nice to have.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: I've got a bunch of clothes and dresses that my sisters are giving me. They are out of style and I hate to get rid of them and I think that I'll keep them and make something with them. It would be neat to make a quilt out of all of them.

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: Yes, if you can.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: You are still quilting now? Is that what you do when you relax?

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: Yeah. That quilt that I showed you in there on the bed, I just got done quilting that. I'm making that for a friend of 21 mine and I did it that evening and I enjoyed it.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: You make something like that and it's so beautiful and it's so precious and you give it away.

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: Well, that belongs to somebody else, anyway. It's all finished except for the ruffle. She just lives up here a ways, but they own a place way up the Clearwater. They own a place up near where I used to live. When my husband died, she was nice to me and invited me up. After you've been married 50 years, it's kind of a turn around thing when something happens like that. So, she invited me up there and I was up there a couple of times and I offered to do that quilt for her. That took about a month or six weeks, but I just did it when I wanted to. I didn't work at it too much at one time but I enjoyed it. Now I'm hunting around for another one, I'd like to make another one. I'd like to quilt another one and I quilt it on a hoop. I don't put it up on the frame because it kind of takes up the whole room. And another thing, you can't do it very good by yourself, you know, you can't turn the things very good.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: Do you watch TV when you quilt?

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: It runs.

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: I don't care too much about TV.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: Do you ever watch movies or anything, or do you ever watch "The Waltons?"

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: Yes, and that's something that put me in mind. My son and I were talking about that. He lives in San Francisco and we were talking about that; it's supposed to be a depression picture and he said, "Well, Mother, they lived a lot better than we lived in the depression." Now, you see, he remembers -- they lived in a better house than we did. We have the same principles as they have, a lot of little unusual things in there that come up. The "Little House on the Prairie" is the same way. And we'd have lots of those good principles, you know, well, we lived that way. Yet they had better things. I think they had a better home than we did. Boy, we lived in horrible places! Now, I don't mean that it made any effect on our personalities or anything. We were always striving for something better. We felt that way. I don't think we ever thought of it; we just lived from day to day and strived for something better. If we got a chance, we'd take something better. Now, when Harry and I come here 32 years ago, the bank had closed on us and we were flat broke. We had saved up a little money and we come down here to Lewiston and bought this piece of ground with an old house on it and we knew the house wasn't any good, but we lived in it just as the same as anybody else would. Tried to keep it clean and neat, tried to be neat. I can't remember us dwelling on things like that. 23

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: Do you ever watch any of the musical shows on TV?

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: Yeah, I like music better than I do some of the shows.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: Do you ever watch "Masterpiece Theater?"

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: Yeah, they are filmed in Moscow someplace, don't they?

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: I think so, yeah.

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: Some of those plays. I like those where they discuss things, the events of the day. I like those, but lots of people don't care for them. I like "60 Minutes." That gives me ... they gather it and it's all there so I can know it.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: Do you like wildlife shows or shows about animals?

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: I watch every wildlife show I can.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: Sometimes on Saturday and Sunday on nights they have them on for a couple of hours.

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: Yes, and I watch every one of them. I love those because I have lived outside, I suppose is the reason why. Say, have you heard anything about this Carla Emery that is writing this book? Carla Emery gave me one of her books; she's writing on country living. 24

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: I haven't even heard about it.

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: Well, it's very unusual.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: Where does she live?

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: She lives up in Kendrick. That's one of them, $12.95 for that.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: It's on recipes?

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: Well, she has a few recipes in there, but it's mostly on country living. She tells about how to do everyday chores while you are living out. Of course, she's run into a snag; she wants to make kind of a commune up there in Kendrick. She wants to buy four or five hundred acres of ground and make a commune, but they don't ...

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: Does she still have copies? Does she sell them?

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: Yeah, they are $12.95. I'll have to write her name down. She's in Kendrick?

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: Yeah, Carla Emery, Kendrick, Idaho. No box number, really. She tells about home brewed beverages, all about how to make them and she gives a few little recipes, not too many. 25

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
words: But there's a lot of history in there, isn't there?

speaker: Myrtle Cressler Warren
words: Yeah, and salt rising bread, she tells all about that.

speaker: Unknown Interviewer
